newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan department stores growing, but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: Japan department stores growing, but for how long?.

text.p: Glimmers of brightness in Japan's economy and posh new malls are luring shoppers back to department stores for everyday needs, industry sources say, but the road to profit is still riddled with uncertainty.

"Many outlets, especially in Tokyo, were revamped to compete against Takashimaya Co Ltd's new shopping mall and sales are improving on the whole," said Masahiro Matsuoka, a senior analyst at Barclays de Zoete Wedd.
"But the number of customers attracted by renovations and new outlets declines with time and with a consumption tax hike coming up, the upswing in profits may be too good to last," he said.
Takashimaya, Japan's oldest department store, said on Monday that it expected its sales to jump at least 26.3 percent to 1.08 trillion yen ($9.5 billion) in the year to February 28, 1997.
Officials said the figure was pushed up by a larger-than-expected stream of crowds at its newly opened entertainment and shopping mall in the heart of Tokyo.
"I think the shoppers' initial enthusiasm towards the new store is lasting longer than originally expected," Takashimaya president Tatsuro Tanaka told a news conference on Monday.
In the first 17 days of operation, Takashimaya officials said the "Times Square" complex brought in 2.9 million customers and 7.9 billion yen ($69.9 million) in sales.
Takashimaya said its half-year parent sales were 511.53 billion yen ($4.52 billion) against 346.23 billion yen ($3.06 billion) a year ago.
Analysts said the most remarkable recovery in the department store sector was likely to be seen by Sogo Co Ltd .

Sogo said its sales rose slightly to 83.35 billion yen ($737.61 million) in the first half of the year. Its parent current loss shrank to 270 million yen ($2.38 million) from 5.79 billion yen ($51.2 million).

"It was battered by the damage caused by the Hanshin Earthquake but its stores in the Kansai area have been rebuilt and business is returning gradually," said Futoshi Saito, a senior analyst at Daiwa Securities.

For the business year, the department store expects sales to grow to 175.0 billion yen ($1.54 billion) from 150.63 billion in this business year, while it expects to turn its parent current loss of 8.33 billion ($73.7 million) to a profit of 100 million yen ($884,000).
Mitsukoshi Co Ltd said earlier this month that its profits were showing moderate rises, led by a rise in sales of designer clothes.
It said its revenues for the first half of the year grew 2.7 percent year on year to 380.04 billion yen ($3.36 billion), while parent current profits tripled to 4.08 billion yen ($36.1 million).

"Clothes, and designer items especially are selling well -- Luis Vuitton sales soared about 46 percent from last year and and Chanel about 27 percent mainly because price differences of imported items have shrunk considerably, making it easier to buy," a Mitsukoshi official said.
Department store officials said that the national sales tax, to be raised from the current three percent to five percent next April, may crop short the signs of recovery in their sales.

"It is a discouraging factor for customers and although there may be large amounts of buying ahead of the increase, it will tighten purse strings in the long run and sales may be affected," the Mitsukoshi official said.
Analysts warn however, the largest threat to the slight upturn in sales and profits forecast for this year may be the economic climate.
"Even though people are beginning to buy again, lured by new stores and cheaper prices, it probably won't take much to make them stop," Matsuoka said. ($=113 yen)
